SCHOOL ROOM · THE ART ROOM · 27 CARDS · AGES 2–5

The Art Room — every card carries a thing to make.

Twenty-seven supplies, twenty-seven activities: draw a picture with shapes, shape a tiny animal, mix two colours together, cut out simple shapes. Every card prints one make-it activity under its name, every supply has its own short page, its own lesson and a printable twin — and the room runs on the youngest rule in the school: make something, make a mess, make it again.

Open the supply shelf ↓The printable set ↗
HOW THIS ROOM WORKS

Read the card. Make the thing. Then go deeper.

Every card in this deck does two jobs: it names one art supply and it prints one activity — a make-it line the card means literally. The short pages on this shelf show each card, quote its activity word for word, and add one way to set the supply up tonight. When one supply becomes a favorite, its lesson page carries the full teaching — what the tool is, what the activity secretly trains, the parent script, the questions to ask — and the library page holds the printable twin with a download button.

The shelf runs in file order like a real room: the drawing tools first, then the paint and print crew, then the cut-and-stick builders, and the studio furniture at the end. For color work beyond this room, the Colors extra class hunts every shade the house hides, and the Coloring Pages keep print-and-color days stocked when the paints are still drying from yesterday.

ALL TWENTY-SEVEN SUPPLIES

Meet the shelf — cover to watercolors.

Every card in the owner’s file order: chalk, clay, colored pencils and cotton balls open the shelf; crayons, paint, scissors and glue carry the middle; and the studio furniture closes it. Tap any card to open its short page.

GAMES THE ART ROOM PLAYS

When the glue is drying, play.

Art time and game time trade places all afternoon, and the school’s games shelf holds the rules for the games this room plays best: the Colour Hunt turns the whole house into a color deck, the Shape Hunt finds the shapes chalk pictures are built from, Shadow Shapes poses drawings against the wall, and Follow the Leader is a copy-me drawing game with no pencil at all. Full rules on every page — the paint pots can wait.

The Colors class is its closest cousin — fifteen spotter sheets for the shades this room paints with — and the Coloring Pages are its quiet corner: bold outlines, one download each, no setup at all.

Making is the curriculum. Every activity on these cards hides real work — grips, pressure, planning, patience — inside something the child thinks is just today’s craft. Do the thing first; the skills follow the glue.

HOLIDAY CRAFTS

Make it for the celebration.

Every holiday needs glue: paper ghosts and painted pumpkins for Halloween, handprint turkeys for Thanksgiving, hearts for Valentine’s Day, crescent moons for Eid. The school’s School Hall keeps the holiday calendar — the next celebration first — and every holiday page there carries printable cards that pair with the make-it activities in this room: craft here, celebrate there.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Chalk — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces chalk through its card activity — drawing a picture with shapes — so the first chalk session builds shape words while it makes art.

What is this?

Chalk is a soft stick of pressed powder that leaves color on rough surfaces: sidewalks, driveways, walls, blackboards. It is the only drawing tool made for the outdoors.

What does it mean?

Drawing with shapes teaches children that pictures are built, not magic: a house is a square with a triangle on top, a sun is a circle with lines. Naming shapes while drawing them is geometry with dusty fingers.

What does the child need to know?

Just chalk and a rough surface you are allowed to mark. Chunky sidewalk chalk fits small fists best; wet chalk draws even brighter.

Why this matters

Shape vocabulary is one of the first math skills a child meets, and chalk gives every shape a giant, washable, no-pressure canvas. Big drawing also feeds the whole-arm movement young shoulders still need.

What it teaches

Shape recognition, shape vocabulary, big-motor drawing, planning ahead (what goes where), and the outdoor cleanup ritual of watching rain erase everything.

Words to learn

chalksidewalkcirclesquaretrianglerectanglewash away

Say this to your child

“"Look at our chalk — it is a big fat stick! Let me see you make marks... strong ones! Now watch: a circle for the sun. A square for the house. A triangle on top — the roof! What does our picture need next?"”

Step by step

  1. Hand over the chalk and let the child make three free marks first — the tool test.
  2. Say the plan: today we build a picture out of shapes.
  3. Draw a big circle together and ask what it could be — sun, ball, face.
  4. Add a square below it and a triangle on top — the house appears.
  5. Ask the child to name each shape as it lands, then let them add the rest of the picture however they like.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, one pink chalk stick lies diagonally — thick in the middle, round on both ends, the exact shape a small fist grips best.

Ask your child

"Which shape is biggest — the circle or the triangle?" "What happens if we draw on the wall? What happens if rain comes?" "Can you draw a circle in the air with your finger?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may narrate every shape out loud, fill the whole driveway before lunch, or discover that chalk on wet ground makes double-bright lines — and demand to keep going.

Out in the real world

Chalk lines mark sports courts, parking spots and hopscotch grids all over town. A child who draws with chalk meets it again at every playground and school blackboard.

Try it together

Shape hop: draw four shapes on the ground and call them out — jump to the triangle, stomp on the circle. The shapes become a game board, and the vocabulary drills itself.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we draw with chalk?" (pictures, shapes) "Name the shapes in our house picture." (square, triangle) "What happens to chalk pictures in the rain?" (they wash away)

This lesson pairs with the Chalk flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Clay — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces clay through its card activity — shaping a tiny animal — so the child meets the oldest art material on Earth as something to build with, not just to squish.

What is this?

Clay is soft earth that holds whatever shape hands give it and keeps that shape as it dries. It rolls into balls, pinches into ears and stands up on the table — unlike anything else on the art shelf.

What does it mean?

Shaping an animal from one ball teaches part-to-whole thinking: a rabbit is a body plus ears plus a nose. Every pinch is a decision, and decisions are where art starts.

What does the child need to know?

Soft clay (air-dry or play clay), a damp cloth to keep it workable, and a table that tolerates crumbs. No tools needed — fingers are the whole toolkit.

Why this matters

Clay builds finger and hand strength better than almost any other art supply, and the strength it builds is exactly the grip writing asks for later. It also teaches patience: the ears only stay if the body was rolled first.

What it teaches

Hand strength, fine-motor control, part-to-whole planning, naming body parts, and the discipline of slow work — clay punishes rushing by falling over.

Words to learn

clayrollpinchpressballearssculpturesoftdry

Say this to your child

“"Here is our ball of clay — soft as a pillow! Roll it, roll it... now it is a body. Pinch, pinch — two ears! We made a rabbit! What should its name be?"”

Step by step

  1. Roll one ball between two palms while saying what you are doing — round and round.
  2. Set the ball down as the body and ask what animal it wants to be.
  3. Pinch two ears up from the top — gently, because clay remembers everything.
  4. Add a nose, eyes or a tail with tiny pressed-on pieces.
  5. Name the animal out loud and give it a spot on the shelf to dry — sculptors always sign and display their work.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a small purple rabbit sits with long ears and a round body — one ball for the body, two pinches for the ears, exactly the sequence the lesson follows.

Ask your child

"Which part did we make first?" (the body) "What did we pinch to make the ears?" "How does the clay feel — hard or soft?" "What happens if we leave it out overnight?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may make a whole zoo one animal at a time, ask to keep the animals on display forever, or discover that flattened clay makes a pancake — which is also an animal, if the family says so.

Out in the real world

Potters, dentists and toy designers all shape soft material into forms — plates, tooth molds, action figures. A child who has shaped clay has already done all three jobs in miniature.

Try it together

Clay bakery: roll snakes and flatten them into pretend bread, cookies and cakes. The same rolling skill now feeds a pretend oven — and counting the cookies sneaks math into the bakery.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do first — roll a ball or pinch ears?" (roll the ball) "Show me how you pinch." "What happens to clay when it dries?" (it gets hard and stays)

This lesson pairs with the Clay flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Colored Pencils — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces colored pencils through the card’s activity — shading a simple object — so the child discovers the flat-side trick that turns a flat drawing into a round one.

What is this?

Colored pencils are thin wooden pencils with colored cores instead of gray graphite. Sharp point for lines, flat side for shading — one tool, two personalities.

What does it mean?

Shading teaches pressure control: light touch makes light color, heavy hand makes dark. Controlling how hard you press is a fine-motor milestone hiding inside a coloring session.

What does the child need to know?

A small set of colored pencils, sharpened, and paper that is not too slick. Short pencils are actually easier for small hands than long ones.

Why this matters

Shading is a child’s first drawing vocabulary word — artists say shading to mean filling with soft color — and the sweep motion trains the same arm control as early handwriting.

What it teaches

Pressure control, wrist movement (the sweep), understanding that pictures can show roundness, and pencil grip — the tripod hold the card’s low grip encourages.

Words to learn

colored pencilsshadesweeplightdarkpressround

Say this to your child

“"Our colored pencils can do a trick! Hold it low and flat — now sweep, sweep, sweep like the wind blowing. Look! The apple is turning red from this side... and look how ROUND it looks!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the two holds: tall like a writing pencil for lines, low and flat for shading.
  2. Draw a big apple outline together — or let the child draw one.
  3. Lay the pencil almost flat and sweep along one side of the apple, light as wind.
  4. Sweep again beside the first strokes and let the color pile up softly.
  5. Compare the two sides — the swept side looks round. Say the word: shading.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a blue box holds a row of sharpened pencils standing point-up — every point the same height, ready for either hold.

Ask your child

"What happens if we press hard?" (dark color) "What about soft and slow?" (light color) "Which side of the apple is darker?" "Can you sweep like the wind?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may sweep everything now — including the carpet with an imaginary pencil — or carefully shade one object for ten quiet minutes, which is a gift, take it.

Out in the real world

Illustrators, architects and designers shade every day: the roundness on a cartoon character, the depth on a house drawing — all built from the same sweep the child just learned.

Try it together

Ramp race shading: draw a hill, shade the side the sun would hit dark and the other side light. The child has just done real light logic with a pencil.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we hold the pencil for shading?" (low and flat) "What makes the color darker?" (pressing harder) "Point to the round side of the apple."

This lesson pairs with the Colored Pencils flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Cotton Balls — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces cotton balls through the card’s activity — dabbing paint to make clouds — so even the youngest artist gets clean, satisfying prints with zero brush skills.

What is this?

A cotton ball is a soft puff of plant fiber that soaks up paint and gives it back in one gentle bounce. No handle, no bristles, no wrong way to hold it.

What does it mean?

Dabbing teaches the print cycle — dip, press, lift — and repeating it builds rhythm. Pattern talk starts here: again, again, same again.

What does the child need to know?

Cotton balls, paint poured on a plate (a little goes far), and paper. A clothespin clipped into the ball gives the fluff a handle for paint-shy fingers.

Why this matters

Cotton ball printing is the friendliest first printmaking: the result is always puffy and cloudlike, so the youngest child gets a win on every press. It also builds the dip-press-lift rhythm every stamp and sponge uses later.

What it teaches

Rhythm and repetition, gentle pressure control, hand-eye timing, and the science habit of noticing — how much paint makes a fat cloud versus a thin one.

Words to learn

cotton balldabdippressliftcloudpuffysoft

Say this to your child

“"Here is our soft cloud maker! Dip it in the paint — press, LIFT! Look, a cloud! Press again... another cloud! Our sky is filling up. What color cloud comes next?"”

Step by step

  1. Let the child squeeze one dry cotton ball first — this is what fluff feels like.
  2. Dip it in the paint and count the dip: one.
  3. Dab on the paper — press down, lift up — and look at the cloud that landed.
  4. Dab again beside it, then above it, until the sky fills.
  5. Try a second color and ask what weather is coming — every cloud color is a forecast.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, three puffy cloud shapes are dabbed in blue — each one made of many small dabs that joined together, which is exactly how real dabs behave.

Ask your child

"How do we make the print — press and what?" (lift) "What happens if we drag the cotton instead?" (a smear — sometimes a good smear) "How many clouds are in our sky?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may dab until the paper goes transparent with paint, discover the clothespin handle and refuse to go back, or declare the finished sky a storm — in which case, boom.

Out in the real world

Print shops, wallpaper makers and wrapping-paper designers all repeat one image many times — the same press-lift-repeat the child is doing with a cotton ball.

Try it together

Weather report: paint a sky, then point at each cloud and give it a weather name — soft cloud, storm cloud, cloud with the sun behind it. Craft becomes meteorology.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we press on the paper?" (the cotton ball) "Show me press and lift." "What did we make?" (clouds) "What is a cotton ball made of?" (cotton — from a plant)

This lesson pairs with the Cotton Balls flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Craft Sticks — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces craft sticks through the card’s activity — building a tiny frame — so the child’s first construction project holds a picture, which is the most motivating cargo possible.

What is this?

Craft sticks are flat, smooth wooden sticks — the popsicle stick’s cleaner cousin. Glued side by side they make boards; glued at the corners they make frames, boxes and fences.

What does it mean?

Building a frame teaches corners: two sticks meeting at a right angle make something sturdy. It also teaches the glue rule — press and wait — the first delay a maker learns to respect.

What does the child need to know?

Craft sticks, white glue, and a picture small enough to live inside. Tape behind the corners holds the square while the glue dries overnight.

Why this matters

Frames turn flat art into objects — something the child can stand up, hold and gift. Making a gift-sized object teaches that art is for giving, and corners are the seed of all box-building to come.

What it teaches

Spatial thinking (corners, squares), glue discipline, patience for drying, and the pride arc of build-then-use: the frame is not the end, the framed picture is.

Words to learn

craft stickframecornersidegluedrystand up

Say this to your child

“"Here are our sticks — smooth like popsicles! Two here, two there... look, a little square window! A dot of glue on every corner — press, press. Now we WAIT. Good things take one sleep."”

Step by step

  1. Lay two sticks up-and-down and two side-to-side to see the square first — dry run.
  2. Dab glue on the end of the first stick and press a corner.
  3. Keep going around: corner, corner, corner, corner.
  4. Tape behind the joints and stand the frame up — does it hold?
  5. Leave it overnight, then slide the small picture in and choose the display spot together.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, four green sticks meet in a neat square — the top and bottom sticks overlap the side sticks, which is the corner trick that makes the frame strong.

Ask your child

"How many sticks does a frame need?" (four) "What holds the corners together?" (glue) "What goes inside our frame?" "Why do we wait for the glue?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may build a second frame the moment the first is done, declare the frame a gift for a grandparent, or test whether the frame holds a small toy — engineering has begun.

Out in the real world

Picture framers, carpenters and toy makers all join corners — doors, windows, birdhouses and bookshelves are frames that grew up. The child’s four sticks are the whole idea, small.

Try it together

Fence and field: glue a row of sticks standing up along the bottom of a paper field, then draw what lives inside. The frame skill becomes a fence, and the farm needs naming.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many sticks make a frame?" (four) "Show me a corner." "What do we do after gluing?" (press and wait)

This lesson pairs with the Craft Sticks flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Crayon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the crayon through its card activity — drawing a colourful picture — and gives the child the honest science of why the world’s first art tool never lets you down.

What is this?

A crayon is colored wax in a paper sleeve: it writes by leaving tiny wax bits on the paper, needs no ink and never dries out. It works tilted, flat, sideways or in a fist.

What does it mean?

Drawing with many colors teaches choosing — which color for the sun, which for the grass — and naming colors out loud builds the vocabulary that sorting games will use later.

What does the child need to know?

A box of crayons and paper. Broken crayons are not broken: their flat sides make excellent rubbings, and short ones train a better grip than long ones.

Why this matters

The crayon is usually the first tool a child controls completely — no water, no caps, no setup — so it is where the habit of making marks on purpose begins. Ten colors on one page is also the friendliest color-naming drill ever built.

What it teaches

Color recognition and naming, grip strength, the choosing muscle, and mark-making confidence — every surface gets tested, which is exploration, not mischief.

Words to learn

crayonwaxcolordrawrainbowpapersleevemarks

Say this to your child

“"Crayons! Pick a color — what is it? Red! Draw the sun. Pick another — green! What is green on our picture? The grass! How many colors have we used? Let’s count them!"”

Step by step

  1. Open the box together and name five colors by pointing — the child points, you both say them.
  2. Ask what the child wants to draw, then which color that thing needs first.
  3. Draw the big things first — sun, house, dog — each in its chosen color.
  4. Count the colors on the page as they land: one, two, three...
  5. Keep going until ten colors are on the page, then declare it officially a rainbow picture.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, one red-orange crayon stands straight up with its wrapper showing — the sleeve is the crayon’s label and its handle, and peeling it is also legal.

Ask your child

"Which color is your favorite today?" "What happens if we draw on top of the red with the yellow?" (new color, sort of) "Can you draw with the crayon lying down flat?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may line the crayons up by color before drawing anything, test every color on one hand, or peel the whole sleeve off one crayon with surgical focus.

Out in the real world

Crayons label bins in classrooms, mark Xs on treasure maps in books, and wait in every restaurant that has ever seated a family. Knowing crayons is knowing childhood’s common language.

Try it together

Color hunt: draw a big yellow circle on paper, then hunt the room for five real yellow things and draw each one inside the circle. The crayon leads the search.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is inside a crayon?" (wax) "Does a crayon dry out?" (no — never) "How many colors are on your picture?" (count together)

This lesson pairs with the Crayon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Drawing Pad — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the drawing pad through its card activity — drawing your favorite thing — and teaches the quiet superpower of a pad: it keeps everything.

What is this?

A drawing pad is a stack of blank pages bound on one side, usually with a spiral. Every page is a fresh start, and the finished pages stay attached — a book that grows.

What does it mean?

Choosing a favorite thing and filling a page with it teaches composition — big things in the middle, details around — and the pad teaches care: pages here are kept, not lost.

What does the child need to know?

A drawing pad with pages big enough for whole-arm drawing, plus whatever drawing tools the child loves. The pad is the supply; the tools can rotate.

Why this matters

A pad builds the idea of a body of work: this drawing matters because it lives next to yesterday’s. That is the earliest version of a portfolio, and looking back through it is the child’s first art review.

What it teaches

Composition (filling a page), decision-making (which favorite), book handling — turning pages gently — and memory: last week’s drawing is still here to talk about.

Words to learn

drawing padpagespiralfavoritefillwhole pagekeep

Say this to your child

“"Here is our drawing pad — a book with no words yet! Open to a new page: what is your favorite thing? A dog! Let’s draw it BIG, right here in the middle. What is next to your dog?"”

Step by step

  1. Open the pad to the first blank page and hold it up — a fresh room.
  2. Ask the big question: what is your favorite thing in the whole world?
  3. Start drawing it together in the middle of the page — big, not tiny.
  4. Fill the space around it: where does it live? What is next to it?
  5. Sign the page (name or scribble), turn back one page and visit last week’s drawing.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a purple spiral-bound pad leans open with a pencil resting on the page — the spiral is the binding that lets the book lie flat or fold all the way around.

Ask your child

"What did we draw on this page?" "Where does the spiral go?" "Can we tear the pages?" (no — they stay) "Which drawing is older — this one or that one?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may turn the pad into a daily diary with one drawing per morning, carry it everywhere like a briefcase, or request that you draw your favorite on the facing page — the pad becomes a conversation.

Out in the real world

Artists keep sketchbooks the same way — every museum’s famous painter owned pads of quick drawings. The child’s pad is a sketchbook with juice stains, which is how the great ones start.

Try it together

Two artists, one book: you draw the favorite thing, the child adds three details, then swap roles on the next page. The pad becomes a relay, and neither artist ever finishes alone.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we keep in the pad?" (our drawings) "Show me how we turn pages." (gently) "What is your favorite thing?" — and watch the answer change weekly.

This lesson pairs with the Drawing Pad flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Easel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the easel through its card activity — setting up the artwork — so the child learns the full artist routine: prepare, paint, step back, look.

What is this?

An easel is a stand that holds paper upright while the artist works: clips on top, paint pots or a ledge below, and three or four legs to keep it steady. It is furniture for making things.

What does it mean?

Setting up teaches the routine before the art: paper first, then tools, then work. Standing to paint also changes the body — big shoulder movements replace small wrist ones.

What does the child need to know?

An easel (or a clipboard propped on a chair), paper, clips, and paint or markers. The setup is the lesson: let the child do every step.

Why this matters

The step-back-and-look habit is the most professional thing an artist does, and children learn it naturally at an easel — the work is at arm’s length, so viewing it means moving. That tiny habit is real self-evaluation, learned at two.

What it teaches

Sequencing (setup before art), big-motor strokes, independence — every step is child-sized — and the observing habit of stepping back to see the whole picture.

Words to learn

easelclipstanduprightstep backlookartiststudio

Say this to your child

“"This is our easel — real artists use these! Clip the paper... snap! Paint here, brush here. Now make big strokes — your whole arm is painting! Step back with me... LOOK at it. What does it need?"”

Step by step

  1. Bring the paper to the easel together and let the child work the clip — it is a finger workout.
  2. Set out the paints or markers below, one at a time, naming each choice.
  3. Stand beside the easel and paint or draw — whole arm, big strokes.
  4. Step back together two steps and look: what does the picture need now?
  5. Finish with the official artist move: one more look from far away, then sign it.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, an orange easel stands on three legs with a blank canvas clipped at the top — the empty canvas is the invitation, and the ledge below is where the paint waits.

Ask your child

"What holds the paper tight?" (the clip) "Why do artists step back?" (to see the whole picture) "Show me a big easel stroke." "Where does the paint sit when we are not using it?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may announce "I’m working" and expect no interruptions, step back after every single stroke, or set up a stuffed animal beside the easel as a student — the studio now has staff.

Out in the real world

Every painter in every museum paints at an easel, and street portrait artists set theirs up in parks. The word easel comes from donkey — the patient animal that carries the load.

Try it together

Gallery hour: finish the easel painting, step all the way back, and walk the room past it like a visitor. Someone buys it — for a pretend number, paid in hugs.

Understanding check

Ask: "What goes on first — paper or paint?" (paper) "Show me stepping back to look." "What does the clip do?" (holds the paper)

This lesson pairs with the Easel flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Eraser — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the eraser through its card activity — erase and redraw a shape — so the child learns early that paper offers unlimited second drafts.

What is this?

An eraser is a soft rubber block that lifts pencil marks off paper: rubbing picks the graphite up into little roll-aways. It works on pencil, not on markers — and that difference is a lesson itself.

What does it mean?

Erase-and-redraw teaches revision: the first line was information, the second line is the choice. Children who erase freely keep drawing bravely — the eraser is what makes bold lines safe.

What does the child need to know?

A white or pink eraser, pencil drawings to revise, and a rule worth teaching: rub gently, or the paper rubs too. Crumbs brush away with the side of the hand.

Why this matters

Fear of the wrong line freezes young artists; the eraser removes the fear. But the deeper lesson is that redrawing is normal — every book, every logo, every movie went through erasers first.

What it teaches

Revision thinking, gentle pressure (the opposite of marker force), fine wrist motion for the rub, and the emotional skill of changing course without frustration.

Words to learn

erasereraserubredrawcrumbssecond trygently

Say this to your child

“"Here is our magic block — the eraser! Draw a shape... now rub, rub, GENTLY — look, it is going away! Poof! Now draw it again, any way you want. Paper always gives us another try."”

Step by step

  1. Draw a circle in pencil — deliberately imperfect is perfect here.
  2. Rub the eraser across it gently and watch the circle lift away.
  3. Brush the crumbs with the side of the hand — the table resets.
  4. Redraw the shape, changed on purpose: a moon, a C, a cookie with a bite.
  5. Ask which one the child likes better — both answers are correct; the choosing is the point.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a yellow eraser lies beside little curled crumbs — those rolls are the pencil it picked up, proof that the mark did not vanish, it moved.

Ask your child

"Can we erase marker?" (no — why not?) "How do we rub — hard or gentle?" (gentle) "Where did the circle go?" (into the crumbs) "What did we draw the second time?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may erase entire pages for the joy of the reset, blow every crumb off the table like a tiny storm, or start drawing bolder immediately — the safety net is working.

Out in the real world

Designers, writers and engineers all revise — the pencil-and-eraser pair is still on every architect’s desk. And before rubber erasers, people erased with soft bread.

Try it together

Before and after: draw a house, erase one part, and redraw it better — a bigger door, a round window. Frame the two versions side by side: the eraser made the difference, and the child can point to it.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the eraser lift off the paper?" (pencil) "Show me a gentle rub." "What do we do after erasing?" (draw again)

This lesson pairs with the Eraser flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Feathers — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces feathers through the card’s activity — gluing a colourful texture — so the child’s picture gains something real to touch, which flat art cannot do alone.

What is this?

Feathers are a bird’s coat: soft at the base, smooth along the vane, and colored without any paint. On the craft table they are texture — the part of a picture your finger wants to visit.

What does it mean?

Gluing feathers teaches two-step craft thinking: dot of glue, press, hold. It also teaches texture as a word — this part is soft, this part is flat paper — a real art term, learned by fingertip.

What does the child need to know?

Craft feathers, white glue, and paper or a cardboard base. A small pot of glue with a brush or cotton swab keeps the dots reasonable.

Why this matters

Feathers invite the softest kind of noticing: children hold one, feel both sides, and start asking the bird questions. Craft that carries real nature into it builds the bridge between art time and the outdoors.

What it teaches

Glue control, two-step sequences, texture vocabulary (soft, smooth, fluffy), counting as feathers land, and gentle handling — feathers tear, so the hands learn calm.

Words to learn

feathersoftsmoothtexturegluepresswingbird

Say this to your child

“"Here is a feather — feel it! So soft one way, smooth the other. A dot of glue... press... one, two, three, four, five. Stuck! Our picture has real feathers now — a bird that never flies away!"”

Step by step

  1. Hold one feather up and feel both sides together — soft this way, smooth that way.
  2. Draw or choose the picture that will wear the feathers — a bird, a hat, a letter.
  3. Dab a small glue dot where the first feather lands.
  4. Press the feather’s base into the dot and count to five.
  5. Add the next feather beside it, then compare: which feather is longest? Pretend to count the whole wing.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, one big teal feather lies on its side — the middle line is the shaft, the flat parts on both sides are the vanes, and the bottom is the soft down that held the bird warm.

Ask your child

"How does the feather feel?" "Which side is softer?" "What animal grows feathers?" "How many feathers are on our picture?" "What happens if we blow the feather into the air?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may glue a feather colony across the whole page, blow feathers off the table and chase them, or stroke the finished picture every time they pass — the texture is doing its job.

Out in the real world

Pillows, jackets and comforters are stuffed with feathers — the same softness, doing the same job. And birds preen their feathers daily, which is a bird doing its own craft maintenance.

Try it together

Feather float: drop one feather from up high and watch it drift, then fan paper to keep it in the air. The craft supply becomes air science without leaving the table.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we put under the feather before pressing?" (a dot of glue) "Show me soft and smooth sides." "Who grows feathers?" (birds)

This lesson pairs with the Feathers flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Glue — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces glue through its card activity — making a paper collage — and installs the two rules that keep every future craft day sane: dots not rivers, press and wait.

What is this?

White glue is a liquid that grips by drying: its water evaporates, the rest hardens, and two things stay joined. It is the connective tissue of the whole art shelf.

What does it mean?

A collage teaches arrangement — which piece goes where, what touches what — and glue adds the discipline of waiting: the pieces only stay if the hands give them time.

What does the child need to know?

White glue, paper pieces (torn magazine pages work beautifully), and a base sheet. Glue sticks are tidier for tiny hands; the bottle is better for teaching the dot.

Why this matters

Collage is composition without drawing skills — anyone can arrange — so it gives every child a full art win. And learning that wet glue needs time is the child’s first material science: change takes a while.

What it teaches

Arrangement and composition, glue-quantity judgment, patience for drying, tearing strength, and the two-hand coordination of hold-press-count.

Words to learn

gluedotcollagetearpresswaitdrystick

Say this to your child

“"Here is our glue — it is the helping liquid! A little dot... another dot... NO rivers today! Press the paper down — one, two, three... ten! Stuck! Now it needs time to dry. What goes on next?"”

Step by step

  1. Tear or cut the paper pieces first — a little pile of color.
  2. Say the rule together: dots, not rivers.
  3. Place one dot, press one piece, count to ten.
  4. Build the collage outward — big pieces first, small pieces in the gaps.
  5. Leave it flat to dry and guess how long — then check the guess later.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a purple glue bottle stands ready with one drop at the tip — one drop is the whole message: glue is powerful, so it travels in small amounts.

Ask your child

"How much glue — a dot or a river?" (a dot) "What does glue do when it dries?" (hardens, grips) "What happens if we use too much?" (wrinkles, sliding pieces) "How long should we wait?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may squeeze the entire bottle given one unsupervised second, learn the dot rule in a single session, or press each piece down for a full solemn ten-count — the counting is optional but the pride is not.

Out in the real world

Bookbinders, carpenters, shoe makers and envelope factories all glue for a living — glued things hold the world together, from book spines to the envelope on the mail.

Try it together

Glue-dot dodge: the grown-up makes a "river" of glue on scrap paper and the child fixes it — "too much! dots!" — with their own correct version. Teaching the rule back proves it stuck.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me a glue dot." "What do we do after pressing the paper down?" (wait) "Why did our pieces slide?" (too much glue)

This lesson pairs with the Glue flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Ink — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces ink through the card’s activity — making a fingerprint picture — and lands the quiet wonder: the pattern inside every finger belongs to exactly one person.

What is this?

Ink is liquid color that transfers in copies: touch a pad, press a surface, and the shape of the touch prints itself. A fingerprint prints the tiny ridge lines of the finger itself.

What does it mean?

Fingerprinting teaches the print idea — press, lift, look — and the identity idea: my swirl, your swirl, different every time. Art and selfhood in one press.

What does the child need to know?

A washable ink pad (washable matters — see any toddler), paper, and a pen or marker for adding details. One finger at a time keeps it a game, not a hand-print storm.

Why this matters

Fingerprints connect art to the child’s own body and to the bigger world — doors, phones and detectives all read the same swirls. The print is also the fastest artwork in existence: one second, done, perfect.

What it teaches

Press-and-lift control, noticing fine detail (the swirls), identity vocabulary, one-to-one counting as prints land, and gentle restraint — pressing hard makes a blob.

Words to learn

inkprintfingerprintpressliftswirlpatternunique

Say this to your child

“"Here is our ink pad — one little tap with one little finger! Now press down... and LIFT! Look inside your print — those are YOUR lines, nobody else has them! Press again — the same swirl, every time!"”

Step by step

  1. Press one fingertip gently on the pad — tap, tap.
  2. Press it on the paper and LIFT — look closely: lines! Swirls!
  3. Press again with the same finger and compare: same pattern, new print.
  4. Add pen details to turn prints into animals — legs, ears, smiles.
  5. Make a whole family of prints — every family member one finger each — and match the swirls to their owners.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a big pink heart is pressed from one fingerprint after another — the same print repeated until the repeats became a heart, which is exactly what a row of prints can do.

Ask your child

"How many fingers make one print?" (one) "Are your swirls the same as mine?" (no — look!) "What happens if we press too hard?" (a blob) "What did we turn our prints into?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may ink every fingertip in the room — including the dog’s paw, which is also a print — or study their own swirls for a full quiet minute, which is practically forensics.

Out in the real world

Phones and tablets unlock by fingerprint, doors at big buildings open the same way, and detectives match prints to people. The child’s own swirl is their first ID card.

Try it together

Print parade: one row of thumb prints becomes a caterpillar — draw the face on the first one and legs under each. Count the body parts: how many prints long is the caterpillar?

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we press first — finger or paper?" (finger on the ink) "Show me press and lift." "Does anyone else have your swirls?" (no)

This lesson pairs with the Ink flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Markers — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces markers through the card’s activity — making bold colourful lines — and teaches the two marker disciplines: the cap goes back on, and the line goes all the way.

What is this?

Markers are tubes of liquid ink with a felt tip: touch paper and color flows out with no pressure at all. They make the boldest, smoothest lines in the drawer.

What does it mean?

Bold lines teach commitment — a marker line cannot be erased, so the child learns to move with intention. Line variety (straight, wavy, zigzag) is also pre-writing: letters are just lines that learned manners.

What does the child need to know?

Washable markers, paper with a backing sheet underneath (markers travel through), and the cap rule: finished means capped. Thick tips for small hands, thin tips for details.

Why this matters

Markers give maximum result for minimum strength, which makes them the confidence tool of the drawer — the picture always shows up. The cap ritual, practiced daily, is responsibility in miniature.

What it teaches

Intentional stroke control, line vocabulary (straight, wavy, zigzag, loop), cap discipline, hand strength for the cap click, and sound-symbol play — lines that make noise.

Words to learn

markercapboldlinestraightwavyzigzagsweep

Say this to your child

“"Markers! Cap off — CHEK! Now one bold line, all the way across — don’t stop! Another one, wiggly like a river. Now sharp like lightning — zigzag, zigzag! What sound does YOUR line make?"”

Step by step

  1. Pop the cap together — CHEK! — and name the ceremony.
  2. Draw one long straight line across the whole page without stopping.
  3. Draw a wavy line, then a zigzag — say each one out loud as it lands.
  4. Play the sound game: hum the straight line, drum the zigzag, sing the wave.
  5. Cap it together before the paper changes — the line ends, the cap clicks, done.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, three orange markers stand side by side with their caps on — capped is their resting state, and the whole lesson starts by popping one off.

Ask your child

"What goes back on when we finish?" (the cap) "Can we erase a marker line?" (no — that is why we mean it) "Draw me a zigzag in the air." "Which line sounds like a drum?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may cap every marker with a satisfying click and line them up like crayons, draw sound effects on purpose, or narrate each line — "this one is a ROAR" — which is a sound effects department being born.

Out in the real world

Street painters and sign makers use wide markers for big bold letters, and warehouses mark floors with them. Bold lines that survive outdoors all come from the same felt-tip idea.

Try it together

Line orchestra: lay three long papers on the floor, one per line type. Walk the papers and play each line — stomp the zigzag, glide the wave. The marker game becomes a whole-body concert.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do when we finish a marker?" (cap it) "Show me a bold line." "Name two kinds of lines." (straight, wavy, zigzag — any two)

This lesson pairs with the Markers flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Paintbrush — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the paintbrush through its card activity — painting a bright background — so the child learns the studio order real painters use: color the world first, add the picture after.

What is this?

A paintbrush carries liquid paint from pot to paper on soft hairs: big brush, big wash; small brush, small details. Dipped in water it wakes; wiped on a jar edge it stops dripping.

What does it mean?

Background-first teaches sequencing — the sky before the birds — and the sweep motion (shoulder and elbow, not just fingers) is the big-motor move that early drawing needs.

What does the child need to know?

Paint, brushes (one wide, one small), paper, and a water jar for rinsing. The jar-edge wipe and the paper towel blot are part of the tool, not extra rules.

Why this matters

Painting covers space in a way coloring never does — whole pages turn to sky, sea and sunset in seconds. And the brush teaches the cleanest consequence lesson in art: forget to rinse and every color turns mud.

What it teaches

Big-motor sweeps, color coverage planning, rinse-and-wipe sequencing, brush care, and the patience beat of letting the background dry before the picture lands.

Words to learn

paintbrushbristlespaintsweepbackgroundrinsewashdry

Say this to your child

“"Here is our paintbrush — soft hairs on a stick! Dip... wipe the drip... now SWOOSH, all the way to the edge! Again — we are painting the whole SKY! Rinse the brush before the new color — swish, swish!"”

Step by step

  1. Meet the brush: squeeze the bristles gently — soft like a cat’s ear.
  2. Dip, wipe the drip on the jar edge, then make one big sweep to the paper’s edge.
  3. Cover the whole page top to bottom — the background comes first.
  4. Rinse before every new color: swish, swish, wipe. Watch the water change.
  5. Let it dry, then draw the picture ON TOP of the background — the sky holds the birds now.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a yellow brush points bristles-down — the bristles are the hairs that carry the paint, and the metal band is the ferrule that holds them to the handle.

Ask your child

"What carries the paint?" (the bristles) "What do we do between colors?" (rinse) "What happens if we forget to rinse?" (mud!) "Show me a sweep that reaches the edge."

What your child can say or do

Your child may rinse so enthusiastically that the jar needs emptying twice, paint every background sunset-orange for a week, or forbid anyone from drawing before the background dries — the studio has rules now.

Out in the real world

House painters, sign writers and museum painters all work background first — walls, signs, skies. The rinse jar sits on every real painter’s table, exactly where it sits at yours.

Try it together

Sky diary: paint one background each Monday for a month — gray sky, orange sky, blue sky — and date the corner. The backgrounds become a weather record painted by its own witness.

Understanding check

Ask: "What comes first — background or picture?" (background) "Show me the rinse move." "What part of the brush holds the paint?" (the bristles)

This lesson pairs with the Paintbrush flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Palette — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the palette through its card activity — mixing two colours together — so the child’s first chemistry set is a tray of paint.

What is this?

A palette is the flat tray where a painter holds and mixes colors — the card’s has paint spots and the famous thumb hole. Mixing is the palette’s whole job: two colors go in, one new color comes out.

What does it mean?

Mixing teaches the biggest idea in color: colors are not fixed — they combine and change. Predicting the result (what will red and yellow make?) is a real scientific guess, tested with a swirl.

What does the child need to know?

Paint in at least red, yellow and blue, a mixing surface (the palette, a plate, a washed lid), and a spoon or brush for stirring. White and black stretch the game later.

Why this matters

The primary colors are the child’s first system with rules: three colors can make nearly everything. Mixing also builds prediction language — "I think... it made!" — guess, test, result, the whole scientific method in one thumbprint of paint.

What it teaches

Prediction and testing, color vocabulary (primary, new color), stirring coordination, cause and effect, and the sharing ritual — mixing is always better with two spoons.

Words to learn

palettemixstirswirlorangegreenpurplenew color

Say this to your child

“"Here is our palette — the color laboratory! Red and yellow are going in... stir, stir, swirl... what will come out? Look — ORANGE! You MADE a color! What should we mix next?"”

Step by step

  1. Name the primaries together: red, yellow, blue — the colors that make others.
  2. Ask the guess: what do red and yellow make? Listen to every prediction.
  3. Squeeze both onto the palette and stir — round and round.
  4. Reveal: ORANGE. Compare it to the guess — close? Better?
  5. Repeat with blue and yellow (green) and red and blue (purple), keeping the chart of results.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a green palette holds round paint spots with one empty curve — that missing notch is the thumb hole, where the painter’s thumb grips while the hand mixes.

Ask your child

"Which colors did we mix today?" "What did red and yellow make?" "What do you THINK blue and red will make?" (guess first!) "Where does the thumb go on the palette?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may mix everything into one celebrated brown — a classic, honor it — or start predicting colors for the whole pantry: "banana and blueberries make... green!"

Out in the real world

Paint stores mix every shade a customer brings in, bakers mix colors into frosting, and screen makers mix light instead of paint. Mixing is a working skill in three different jobs.

Try it together

Secret recipe: the grown-up mixes a mystery color, and the child detective names the ingredients — "orange! red and yellow!" — then swaps roles. The lab takes turns being the scientist.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do red and yellow make?" (orange) "What do blue and yellow make?" (green) "Show me the stir." "Where do the colors mix?" (on the palette)

This lesson pairs with the Palette flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Paper Plate — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the paper plate through its card activity — turning it into a funny face — the friendliest portrait lesson any child ever takes.

What is this?

A paper plate is a flat round of sturdy card: strong enough to hold paint and glue, already shaped like the head most pictures need. Its rim is a ready-made frame; its middle is a face.

What does it mean?

Making a face teaches placement — eyes up top, nose in the middle, mouth below — the same body-map a child is building in their own head. The plate is a mirror for learning where faces keep their parts.

What does the child need to know?

Paper plates, drawing tools, glue, and any loose parts: buttons, yarn, paper scraps, bottle caps. Flipping the plate to its back gives a smoother canvas.

Why this matters

Faces are the thing humans read earliest and best, so building one is practicing a survival skill as old as childhood. And the plate’s roundness breaks the rectangle habit — art does not have to be square.

What it teaches

Face-part placement, layering (draw, then glue, then add), round-format composition, naming feelings as the face changes, and fine-motor work with small glued parts.

Words to learn

paper plateroundfaceeyesnosemouthrimsilly

Say this to your child

“"Here is our plate — turn it over... LOOK, it is already a face! Where do the eyes go? Up top! The nose? Right in the middle! Now the silliest smile we can draw... what kind of face is this — happy? Surprised? SILLY?"”

Step by step

  1. Flip the plate and look at it — what shape is this? A circle! What could it be?
  2. Ask where the eyes go and let the child place them — high, high up.
  3. Draw or glue the nose in the middle, then the mouth below.
  4. Add the extras: yarn hair, button freckles, a paper-tube nose that sticks out.
  5. Hold the finished face in front of your own and let it talk — every funny face needs its voice.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a pink plate shows its rim marked like a sunburst — the rim is the plate’s edge and, on a face, the perfect spot for hair, ears and hats.

Ask your child

"Where do the eyes go?" (top) "Where does the nose go?" (middle) "What shape is the plate?" (a circle) "What feeling is your face showing now?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may build a whole family of plates — one per person, including the cat — or swap the mouth on demand: "now make it surprised!" Portrait work, on request.

Out in the real world

Masks, clocks, targets and party decorations are all plate-shaped crafts, and the plate itself was invented when a card factory noticed its scraps made perfect lunch carriers.

Try it together

Feeling parade: make four plates — happy, sad, surprised, sleepy — and hold up the right one as you tell a little story. "Then the ice cream fell... which face?" The plates answer.

Understanding check

Ask: "What shape is our plate?" (circle) "Where does the nose go?" (middle) "Show me your plate’s silliest smile."

This lesson pairs with the Paper Plate flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Paper — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces paper through its card activity — folding a simple animal — so the child discovers the magic angle: folding turns flat paper into sculpture with no glue at all.

What is this?

Paper is the art shelf’s starting material — and folding is its superpower. One crease makes a card; two make ears; three can make the paper stand. The card’s orange dog began as one flat square.

What does it mean?

Folding teaches transformation: same paper, new animal, changed by hands alone. Following fold-by-fold is also the child’s first real procedure — step one, then step two, in order, or the ears are wrong.

What does the child need to know?

Paper squares (copy paper cut down works), a table edge for crisp creases, and hands. Sticker paper and magazine pages fold too — any paper is an animal waiting.

Why this matters

Folding builds spatial thinking — the child must see the ear before it exists — and it is the quietest possible craft: no mess, no setup, restaurant-table ready. The one-sheet rule also teaches that limits make games.

What it teaches

Sequential steps, crease control (press with the whole finger), symmetry (both ears the same), prediction — what will this fold make? — and the pride of a standing result.

Words to learn

paperfoldcreasecornertrianglestandearsorigami

Say this to your child

“"Here is our paper — flat as a pancake. Fold it... press the crease, PRESS! Now fold the corners up — ears! Stand it up... LOOK! A little animal is standing on the table! What sound does it make?"”

Step by step

  1. Fold the square corner to corner and press the crease hard — one stroke, one line.
  2. Look at the triangle together: what animal could this be? A cat?
  3. Fold the two top corners up — the ears arrive.
  4. Turn it over and stand it on its flat bottom — it stands! Draw the face.
  5. Name the animal and make its sound — every folded animal gets a voice.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, an orange dog stands folded from one square sheet — its ears, tail and legs are all creases, nothing cut, nothing glued: the whole animal lives in the folds.

Ask your child

"What changed the paper into an animal?" (folds) "Show me how we press a crease." "Can our animal stand?" (yes — why?) "How many sheets did we use?" (one)

What your child can say or do

Your child may fold everything for a day — napkin animals at dinner, newspaper hats — or invent a brand-new animal by accident and insist it is real. It is real.

Out in the real world

Origami artists, box makers and paper engineers who design pop-up books all fold for a living — and every paper airplane in every classroom is the same skill, flying.

Try it together

Folded zoo: each family member folds one animal in three minutes, then the zoo opens — every animal on display gets its sound performed. Ticket price: one hug.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do to make ears?" (fold the corners) "Show me a crease." "Did we use glue?" (no — just folds) "What is paper folding called?" (origami)

This lesson pairs with the Paper flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Pencil — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the pencil through its card activity — sketching a simple face — the drawing that needs no color, no setup and no courage: just an oval and two dots.

What is this?

A pencil is a wooden barrel around a gray core of graphite and clay: it writes in lines that can be erased, layered and drawn over. It is the tool artists reach for first.

What does it mean?

A face is the highest-value drawing in childhood — it is always somebody. Building one from an oval, dots and a smile teaches that big things are made of small shapes, and feelings change with one line.

What does the child need to know?

A pencil, paper, and an optional mirror for the self-portrait round. The eraser is this lesson’s silent partner — first drafts welcome.

Why this matters

Faces are what children draw most and what portraits are made of, and the pencil’s erasability makes it the right first tool for the attempt. One mouth change turns happy to surprised — the line between feelings is one curve, which is worth knowing early.

What it teaches

Shape composition (oval, dots, curve), pressure control for light sketch lines, feelings vocabulary drawn on demand, and observation — the mirror makes the child look closely at a face they see daily.

Words to learn

pencilsketchovalfaceeyessmilesurprisedgrumpy

Say this to your child

“"Here is our pencil — quiet and gray. Draw a big oval... an egg! Two eyes up top, a little nose, and a mouth... wait, is it happy? Make it happier! Now SURPRISED — a big O mouth! You drew a whole person!"”

Step by step

  1. Draw a big oval together — an egg shape, side to side, not too small.
  2. Add two eyes: dots or circles, up in the top half.
  3. A small curve for the nose, then one line for the mouth — is it smiling?
  4. Change the mouth three times: happy, surprised (a circle O), grumpy (curved down).
  5. Hold up the mirror and sketch the real model — hair first, nobody’s hair is an oval.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a teal pencil lies sharpened to a point — the point is the graphite showing, and the wooden cone around it was carved away by a sharpener.

Ask your child

"Where do the eyes go?" (top half) "How do we make a surprised face?" (O mouth) "What does the pencil make — colors or gray lines?" (gray) "Who did we draw?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may draw the whole family one oval at a time, give every portrait a different mouth on request, or study their own face in the mirror with new suspicion — the mirror does that.

Out in the real world

Portrait artists at fairs and museums start every face with the same oval the child just drew. And every comic book character began as pencil lines before the ink arrived.

Try it together

Feeling dice: draw six faces with six mouths, roll a die, and perform the feeling that lands. The sketch page becomes a theater, and the mouths are the script.

Understanding check

Ask: "What shape is the face?" (oval) "Show me a surprised mouth." (O) "What is inside a pencil?" (graphite) "What do we draw first?" (the big oval)

This lesson pairs with the Pencil flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Ribbon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces ribbon through the card’s activity — making a colourful line collage — so the child’s picture gains lines with actual shape: loops, bends and swoops in 3-D.

What is this?

Ribbon is a narrow strip of cloth that bends, loops and holds a curve. It is shiny, floppy and impossible to draw a straight line with — which is exactly why it is interesting.

What does it mean?

Collaging ribbon teaches the difference between drawn lines and real ones: a pencil line looks like a curve, a ribbon IS a curve. Line vocabulary — loop, zigzag, squiggle — becomes physical.

What does the child need to know?

Ribbon lengths (a hand-span long works best), white glue or a glue stick, and a paper base. Shorter pieces glue flat; long ones insist on loops, which is fine.

Why this matters

Ribbon is often a first sewing-box encounter, and it carries pre-writing geometry: every letter shape the child will one day write is a line — straight, curved, looped — practiced here in ribbon.

What it teaches

Line vocabulary, bend-and-hold finger work, glue-then-place sequencing, planning (what will this line become?), and the big-motor bonus round: ribbon waving in the air.

Words to learn

ribbonbendloopcurvelinecollagewavetail

Say this to your child

“"Here is our ribbon — look how it bends! Swoop! Make a big loop... now a squiggle... now a zigzag! A dot of glue — press. Our ribbon stays exactly where we bent it. What is YOUR ribbon going to be?"”

Step by step

  1. Hold a ribbon high and make one big loop in the air — the shape test.
  2. Lay three ribbons on the paper and decide together what each one is: road? river? rainbow?
  3. Glue under the first ribbon — dots along its path — and press it down.
  4. Keep bending and gluing until the lines make a picture.
  5. Take the leftover ribbon outside and run with it — air lines count too.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a blue bow sits with two long tails — a bow is ribbon’s favorite trick: one pull and the whole thing tightens or lets go.

Ask your child

"Can a ribbon stand up straight?" (only for a second!) "What did your ribbon become?" "Which line is longer — the ribbon or the pencil line?" "Show me a loop with your finger."

What your child can say or do

Your child may ribbon-wave through the whole house wearing the leftover length like a tail, or glue loops so tall the page becomes a maze — follow the finger, find the exit.

Out in the real world

Gift wrappers, dancers (rhythmic gymnasts wave ribbon on a stick) and book binders all use ribbon’s bend. Every wrapped present with a bow on it is this lesson, tied.

Try it together

Line family: draw a pencil line, a crayon line and a marker line on one page, then glue a ribbon line beside them. Ask which line the finger likes best — the finger always votes ribbon.

Understanding check

Ask: "What can ribbon do that pencil cannot?" (bend for real, stand up) "Show me a loop." "What do we put under the ribbon before pressing?" (glue)

This lesson pairs with the Ribbon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Ruler — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the ruler through its card activity — drawing three straight lines — the first tool lesson where two hands learn to work as a team.

What is this?

A ruler is a straight edge with tick marks and numbers: hold it flat, run a pencil along it, and the wobbliest hand in the house draws straight. Flip it over and it is also a counting strip.

What does it mean?

Drawing with a ruler teaches tool partnership — one hand holds, one hand draws — the same two-hand coordination used for cutting later. The numbers on the edge are counting practice that never announces itself.

What does the child need to know?

A ruler (plastic survives toddlers), paper, pencil. The hold matters: palm flat across the middle, fingers away from the drawing edge.

Why this matters

Straight lines are the skeleton of houses, tables, roads and letters. And the ruler teaches an honest tool truth: the right tool makes hard things easy — a lesson that generalizes to scissors, spatulas and hammers.

What it teaches

Two-hand coordination, pressure (hold the ruler firm or it slides), line control along an edge, number recognition along the ticks, and planning — how many lines does a table need?

Words to learn

rulerstraightedgeholdtick marksnumberslineslide

Say this to your child

“"Here is our ruler — the straight-line helper! Press it down FLAT... now ride the pencil along the edge... whoosh! A perfectly straight line! Again! Two hands, one team — hold and draw!"”

Step by step

  1. Wobble a freehand line first — look how it dances. Now for the fix.
  2. Place the ruler flat and press it down with the whole palm.
  3. Ride the pencil along the edge, slow — one perfectly straight line.
  4. Draw three lines: short, long, and one that crosses them both.
  5. Slide a finger along the numbers — count one to ten together, then ask what a table would need.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a blue ruler stands on its end with tick marks up the side — each little mark is the same distance from the last, which is what makes the numbers honest.

Ask your child

"What does the ruler give us?" (straight lines) "Which hand holds and which hand draws?" "What do the little marks on the side do?" (measure) "What happens if we don’t press the ruler?" (it slides!)

What your child can say or do

Your child may measure everything in sight — the cat gets measured, accept it — or draw entire cities out of straight lines, one pressed edge at a time.

Out in the real world

Carpenters, builders and seamstress tables all hold a straight edge while they work — walls, shelves and hems all start as a line that had to be straight. The ruler is two thousand years of that.

Try it together

Line city: draw straight-line roads, a table with four legs and a ladder with a dozen rungs — each drawn on the ruler’s edge. Count the rungs when the ladder is done.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we press down so it doesn’t slide?" (the ruler) "Show me the hold-and-draw team." "How many straight lines did we draw?" (three)

This lesson pairs with the Ruler flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Scissors — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces scissors through the card’s activity — cutting out simple shapes — with the grip, the rhythm and the safety rules that make cutting a victory lap, not a worry.

What is this?

Scissors are two sharp blades on two handles: one thumb up top, fingers below, and every open-close snips the paper between them. They are the strongest tool in the craft box.

What does it mean?

Cutting teaches cause and effect with a real machine: grip, squeeze, result. It also builds the hand arch strength that writing demands — cutting practice is writing practice in disguise.

What does the child need to know?

Child safety scissors (paper only), paper strips and shapes, and the two rules: paper only, and walking feet while holding them. Sitting down is the cutting position.

Why this matters

Cutting is a milestone skill teachers watch for, and it is the first tool that demands thumb-up orientation — the same position a pencil grip wants. Confidence with scissors opens every craft that follows.

What it teaches

Hand strength and arch control, bilateral coordination (both hands: one cuts, one holds the paper), snip rhythm, shape following, and the discipline of tool rules.

Words to learn

scissorssnipcutthumbopencloseshapescareful

Say this to your child

“"Scissors! Thumb on top — open... close... snip! Cut along the line... slowly... look, a square is coming out! Snips make shapes. What shape comes next?"”

Step by step

  1. Fit the hand: thumb in the small hole ON TOP, fingers in the big hole below.
  2. Practice the motion in the air — open... close... snip, snip.
  3. Cut a fat straight strip first: one confident snip at a time.
  4. Follow a drawn line around a big square — slow snips make smooth corners.
  5. Try the wavy snake line last, then sort the shapes: circle, square, snake.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, teal scissors stand open with blades up — the two handles show the thumb hole and the finger hole, the exact fit the lesson starts with.

Ask your child

"Where does the thumb go?" (small hole, on top) "What do scissors cut?" (paper — only paper) "Show me open and close." "What do we do when we carry scissors?" (walk, points down, or hand them over handles-first)

What your child can say or do

Your child may cut confetti until the whole floor sparkles, walk the house with scissors pointed down like a tiny professional, or cut one perfect circle and gasp at it — the gasp is mandatory.

Out in the real world

Barbers, tailors, doctors and paper mills all work with scissors or their bigger cousins — shears. Every haircut and every hem is the same open-close the child just learned, scaled up.

Try it together

Confetti factory: cut the day’s snippets into a jar, and when the jar is full, the confetti launches onto one glue-covered page — the mess becomes the mosaic, planned all week.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which finger goes on top?" (thumb) "What do we cut?" (paper) "Show me a snip." "Where do we walk with scissors?" (carefully — or we sit to cut)

This lesson pairs with the Scissors flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Sponge — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the sponge through its card activity — printing a repeating pattern — the youngest child’s first wallpaper factory.

What is this?

A sponge is full of holes that soak up paint and let it go all at once: one press prints one whole shape. Cut into pieces, one sponge becomes a whole family of stamps.

What does it mean?

Printing teaches the pattern unit — same shape, again and again — the seed of all pattern reading. And the press-lift motion teaches the lift: leave it down and every print is a smudge.

What does the child need to know?

A damp sponge (dry soaks, damp prints), thick paint on a plate, and paper. Cut shapes with scissors for a homemade stamp set — squares and hearts print beautifully.

Why this matters

Patterns are the beginning of math reading: stripes, rows, repeats. Sponge printing shows the child that ONE action, repeated, builds something bigger — the idea behind tiling, knitting and music.

What it teaches

Press-and-lift control, pattern awareness (same, again, row), color planning, hand strength for the press, and the patience of letting prints stay still to dry.

Words to learn

spongeprintpressliftpatternrepeatrowsame

Say this to your child

“"Here is our sponge — press it down... LIFT! A print! Again — press, lift! Press, lift! Look, our prints are marching in a row — same shape again and again. That is a PATTERN. What comes next?"”

Step by step

  1. Feel the sponge — squeeze it damp, watch it spring back.
  2. Dip and press one print, then LIFT straight up — look what landed.
  3. Print a whole row: press, lift, press, lift, saying the rhythm out loud.
  4. Start a second row below — the pattern grows into wallpaper.
  5. Ask the pattern question: what comes next? Then answer it with the sponge.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a green sponge is covered in little round bubbles — the holes are what hold the paint, and they were once the sponge animal’s own channels in the sea.

Ask your child

"What do we say while we print?" (press, lift) "What is a pattern?" (same thing again and again) "What happens if we drag the sponge?" (smudge — try it once, on purpose) "Where do sponges grow?" (in the sea!)

What your child can say or do

Your child may print rows until the paper is full and demand a second sheet, name the pattern — "heart, heart, heart!" — or discover the smudge and decide it is a cloud. It is now a cloud.

Out in the real world

Wallpaper, wrapping paper and fabric factories print patterns all day — one shape, repeated a million times. The child’s row of sponge prints is that factory, hand-powered.

Try it together

Pattern fixer: print a row with one shape missing — star, star, GAP, star — and slide the sponge over. The child finds the break in the pattern, which is the whole skill.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we say when we print?" (press, lift) "What is a pattern?" "Show me lift straight up." "Where do sponges come from?" (the sea — they are animals)

This lesson pairs with the Sponge flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Stamps — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces stamps through the card’s activity — printing a row of shapes — and teaches the two moves that make stamps work: press down hard, lift straight up.

What is this?

A stamp is a shaped surface on a handle: press it into ink or paint, press it on paper, and the shape copies itself perfectly. The card’s stamp prints stars, and every star comes out identical.

What does it mean?

Stamping teaches the copy — same shape, every time — which is pattern and sequence in one game. Borders teach edges: rows that follow the page’s sides are the child’s first layout design.

What does the child need to know?

Stamps (or everyday objects that stamp: corks, Lego bricks, fork tines), an ink pad or thin paint on a plate, and paper. Press firmly and lift straight — that is the whole technique.

Why this matters

Stamping delivers perfect results every time, which makes it the confidence tool of the print family. And the row teaches left-to-right ordering — the same direction reading will one day travel.

What it teaches

Press-and-lift precision, left-to-right row building, pattern planning (star, flower, star, flower), color choices, and the self-checking habit of looking at the row before the next press.

Words to learn

stampinkpressliftrowbordersamecopy

Say this to your child

“"Here is our stamp — tap it in the ink, tap, tap! Press down HARD... and lift straight up — LOOK! A perfect star! Again! A whole row of stars, all the same. What shape joins the parade next?"”

Step by step

  1. Tap the stamp on the ink pad — tap, tap, all four corners.
  2. Press it straight down on the paper — firm, no wiggling.
  3. LIFT straight up — the cleanest star in the house.
  4. Print the whole row, left to right, checking each star as it lands.
  5. Switch stamps and start a second pattern: star, flower, star, flower. The page becomes a border design.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a green stamp prints a row of five stars — each star came from the same stamp, pressed five times: one tool, five identical copies.

Ask your child

"What do we do after pressing down?" (lift straight up) "Why are all the stars the same?" (same stamp!) "Can we wiggle the stamp?" (no — wiggle makes smudges) "What is a row of shapes called?" (a border, a pattern)

What your child can say or do

Your child may stamp every border in the house — book covers, envelopes, their own arm (washable, breathe) — or invent pattern rules and check them out loud: "star, flower, star... next is FLOWER!"

Out in the real world

Post offices, bakeries and warehouses stamp things all day — dates on bread, seals on letters. The very first postage stamp in 1840 was a sticker that let a letter travel the country for a penny.

Try it together

Stamp post office: border a page like an envelope, draw a picture letter inside, stamp a pretend stamp in the corner — and mail it across the table. Delivery is instant; replies are mandatory.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me the two stamp moves." (press down, lift up) "Why did our star smudge?" (we wiggled) "What does the stamp copy?" (the same shape every time)

This lesson pairs with the Stamps flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Stencil — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the stencil through the card’s activity — tracing a simple shape — the tool that lets small hands make big, honest, perfect shapes today.

What is this?

A stencil is a board with a hole cut in it: hold it on the paper and trace the hole, and the shape comes out right every time. The card’s star waits inside its outline.

What does it mean?

Tracing teaches edge-following — the pencil walks the stencil’s edge — and holding-while-tracing is a two-hand team job. The stencil also opens the bigger idea: tools help hands do things they cannot do alone yet.

What does the child need to know?

Stencils (bought or homemade from folded paper), pencils or crayons with tips small enough for the corners, and one rule: the stencil holds still. A sticky-tack dot under each corner helps.

Why this matters

Stencils let a child draw the star they can see in their head but cannot freehand yet — the pride arrives now, the freehand later. Tracing also trains the controlled pencil walks that letters will demand.

What it teaches

Edge following, two-hand cooperation, shape vocabulary (star, heart, circle), controlled pencil pressure, and the confidence loop: perfect shape, made by me, today.

Words to learn

stenciltraceholdedgeholeshapestarcorner

Say this to your child

“"Here is our stencil — a star is hiding inside it! Hold it down tight, tight, tight... now walk the pencil around the edge... slow... slow... LIFT! A perfect star! Your hand made that!"”

Step by step

  1. Look through the stencil hole — the shape is hiding in there.
  2. Press the stencil flat with the helping hand — it must not move.
  3. Walk the pencil slowly around the inside edge, corner by corner.
  4. Lift the stencil — the star is perfect. Cheer honestly.
  5. Slide the stencil a little and trace again: two stars, and the echo game begins.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a blue star outline sits ready — the thick blue edge is the hole’s wall, and the pencil will walk exactly along it, corner to corner.

Ask your child

"What does the helping hand do?" (holds the stencil) "What happens if it moves?" (the shape sneaks away — blurry star) "Which corner is the sharpest?" "What did we make the second time — the same or different?"

What your child can say or do
