Your child may stencil the whole page full of stars and declare it a sky, hold the stencil with such seriousness that it bends, or graduate to drawing the star freehand by the third round — sometimes it happens that fast.

Out in the real world

Sign painters, cake decorators and road crews all use stencils — every crosswalk stripe and birthday-cake letter comes from a held edge. Cave artists blew paint around their hands 30,000 years ago: the first stencil.

Try it together

Echo shapes: trace the star, slide, trace again, slide, trace again — then color the gaps between the stars. One stencil, a whole rainbow echo, and the page hums.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do first — hold or trace?" (hold) "Show me the slow edge walk." "What did the cave artists trace?" (their hands)

This lesson pairs with the Stencil flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Stickers — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces stickers through the card’s activity — making a simple picture — the supply where every placement is a win and the peeling is the secret workout.

What is this?

A sticker is a picture with glue already on its back, protected by a shiny peel-off layer. Peel, press, stuck — the only art supply with no drying time and no wrong strokes.

What does it mean?

Sticker scenes teach placement and overlap — what goes in front of what — and peeling the backing is one of the finest finger exercises ever disguised as fun.

What does the child need to know?

Stickers (bigger is easier), paper or a drawn background, and a patient thumb: the peel is a pinch-roll motion. A grown-up can lift one corner to start the peel, and pride stays intact.

Why this matters

Stickers always succeed, which makes them the confidence supply for the youngest artists — and the drawn-background trick (pencil scene first, stickers move in) turns them into storytelling. Every peel builds the pincer grip writing will ask for.

What it teaches

Pincer grip and peel control, placement decisions, layering (front and behind), scene planning, and the restraint of saving some stickers for tomorrow — a real negotiation.

Words to learn

stickerpeelbackingpressplacescenestuckoverlap

Say this to your child

“"Stickers! Pinch the corner... peel... look, the shiny back! Now press it on our picture — stuck! Where does the next one go? Up in the sky? On the road? Our scene is growing!"”

Step by step

  1. Pick the scene: a garden, a road, the night sky — draw it lightly in pencil first.
  2. Peel the first sticker together — pinch the corner, roll it back.
  3. Press it into the scene and say where it lives: the sun goes UP here.
  4. Keep peeling and placing — what is in front? What is far away?
  5. Leave some stickers on the sheet for tomorrow — the scene continues, and restraint is a skill.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, an orange flower sticker shows six petals around a round center — the peel-away back is what makes it a sticker, and the shine of the backing is how you spot it.

Ask your child

"What do we peel off first?" (the backing) "Show me the pinch and roll." "Where does the sun live in our scene?" "Which sticker is in FRONT?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may sticker everything — the fridge learns boundaries — or arrange one sticker ten times before committing. Both are the skill. The fridge conversation is separate.

Out in the real world

Postage stickers move real mail, price stickers run every shop, and doctors give the champion sticker at every check-up. Stickers are the smallest awards in the world, and they work.

Try it together

Sticker story: place five stickers on a page, then tell the story that connects them — "the cat met the rocket because..." — no wrong order, just plot. The stickers are the cast.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we peel first?" (the backing) "Show me the press." "What did we make — a picture or a scene?" (a scene) "How do stickers stick without glue?" (the glue is already on)

This lesson pairs with the Stickers flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Tape — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces tape through the card’s activity — joining two paper shapes — the instant-gratification fastener that turns flat paper into standing construction.

What is this?

Tape is a strip with sticky on one side: rip off a piece, press it across two things, and they are joined NOW. No drying, no dots, no waiting — tape is glue’s impatient sibling.

What does it mean?

Taping teaches joining — how two things become one structure — and the rip builds a real hand skill: pinch, pull, tear. Tape also makes construction instant, so building momentum stays alive.

What does the child need to know?

Tape (colored masking tape is the child favorite), paper strips and shapes, scissors for clean cuts, and a tape dispenser teaches ripping on the edge — but hand-torn tape is fine and louder.

Why this matters

Tape is the tool that lets young builders keep momentum: chain links, towers, tracks, all held on the spot. And the rip is its own satisfaction — few tools reward effort so loudly.

What it teaches

Ripping strength and control, placing precision (the tape must cross BOTH pieces), construction thinking (what joins to what?), and the follow-through of pressing every inch down.

Words to learn

taperippressjoinsticklinkchainhold

Say this to your child

“"Here is our tape — rip it! RRRIP! Now lay it across both papers — pat, pat, pat. LIFT — they are holding hands! Our papers are stuck NOW, no waiting! How long can our chain get?"”

Step by step

  1. Rip a tape piece together — pinch, pull, RRRIP. Award the sound.
  2. Lay two paper squares edge to edge and lay the tape across both.
  3. Press every bit of the tape down — pat, pat, pat — and test the join: can you lift it?
  4. Tape the next square on — the strip grows into a chain.
  5. Close the chain into a loop and hang the paper chain somewhere official.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, two orange squares are joined in the middle by one strip of tape — the strip crosses both squares, because tape only works when it touches everything it joins.

Ask your child

"What must the tape touch?" (both papers) "Show me the rip." "Do we wait for tape to dry?" (never!) "What did our chain become?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may rip tape into confetti and tape the confetti — a valid art form — or build a paper chain longer than the table, measured on request, defended forever.

Out in the real world

Moving boxes, hospital tubes, package deliveries and car factories all run on tape — it was invented in 1925 for painting two-color cars, and it never left.

Try it together

Tape town: lay colored tape right on the floor in roads and loops, and drive the toy fleet through town. The same joining skill now runs city planning — cleanup peels up in one minute.

Understanding check

Ask: "Does tape need drying time?" (no) "Show me the rip." "Why did our join break?" (the tape missed one paper) "What did we join today?"

This lesson pairs with the Tape flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Watercolors — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces watercolors through the card’s activity — painting a soft sky — where the secret is in the water jar: more water, softer color, calmer painting.

What is this?

Watercolors are paint that wakes up with water: touch a wet brush to a dry pan and the color blooms to life. They go on the paper in see-through washes that blend like weather.

What does it mean?

Watercolors teach the water-to-color relationship — the child controls softness with the jar, not with pressure. They also teach patience: washes need to dry before the next color touches them, or they bleed (sometimes beautifully).

What does the child need to know?

A watercolor set, a brush that holds water, TWO jars (one for rinsing, one clean), and paper that can take a wet wash. The brush drinks water first, then color — that order is the whole technique.

Why this matters

Watercolors are the gentlest paint — they forgive, they blend, they dry light — and they teach the rinse habit that keeps every color honest. Mixing happens on the PAPER, which feels like magic every time.

What it teaches

Water control, brush loading order (water, then color), patience for drying, color observation as washes blend, and the calm that soft painting naturally asks for — watercolor time is quiet time.

Words to learn

watercolorspanwashsoftrinseblendbloomsky

Say this to your child

“"Here are our watercolors — sleepy paints in little pans! Wake one with water... now sweep it across — so soft! More water... even softer! Watch this: wet paper, touch the color... LOOK, it blooms like a flower! We painted weather!"”

Step by step

  1. Wake one pan: brush in water, touch the color, watch it soften.
  2. Load the brush and make one wide sweep across the paper — a soft blue wash.
  3. Add more water to the brush and sweep again — softer still. Compare the two.
  4. For the magic: brush clean water over the whole sky first, then touch color into the wet — it blooms by itself.
  5. Rinse between colors — swish, swish — and let the sky dry flat before the sun lands on it.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a purple box holds six round pans and a brush — each pan is a dry cake of paint that waits for water, and the brush sleeps in its groove.

Ask your child

"What wakes the paint up?" (water) "What makes the color softer?" (more water) "What happens if we forget to rinse?" (every color turns gray-brown — mud) "What did the paint do on the wet paper?" (it bloomed by itself)

What your child can say or do

Your child may become a water-only painter and skip color entirely — valid — or paint sky after sky until the drying rack is a weather system, and narrate every bloom.

Out in the real world

Museum walls hold watercolors centuries old — landscapes, skies and botanical studies painted in exactly these washes. Field sketchers still carry pans in a box like the card’s, one brush, one jar.

Try it together

Sky on demand: paint three small skies — morning (pale), stormy (heavy blue-gray), sunset (orange bleeding into pink) — and guess which real sky each one matches. The paint box becomes a forecast.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we dip the brush in first?" (water) "What makes a wash softer?" (more water) "Show me the rinse between colors." "What did our sky become?"

This lesson pairs with the Watercolors flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.

Chalk

The outdoor artist’s stick: fat, dusty and impossible to hold wrong. The card keeps it simple — circle sun, square house, triangle roof — and the driveway keeps everything until the next rain.

The card’s activity

“Draw a picture with shapes” — printed on the card.

Make it now

Set the supply out and run the card’s activity twice — once slowly, once with full artist confidence. The card is the assignment; the rest of this page is bonus.

Clay

The one supply that stands up on its own. Roll a ball, pinch two ears, and the card’s rabbit arrives one squeeze at a time — the oldest art material on Earth, still the best.

The card’s activity

“Shape a tiny animal” — printed on the card.

Make it now

Set the supply out and run the card’s activity twice — once slowly, once with full artist confidence. The card is the assignment; the rest of this page is bonus.

Colored Pencils

Crayons that grew up: sharper, quieter, full of side-of-the-lead tricks. Lay one almost flat, sweep, and a flat apple turns round — the card’s whole lesson in one motion.

The card’s activity

“Shade a simple object” — printed on the card.

A paintbrush that forgot to be a brush. Dip, dab, lift — the paint lands in puffs, and every puff is a cloud. Two-year-old hands get a win on every single press.

The card’s activity

“Dab paint to make clouds” — printed on the card.
